key_insight: A soft robotic hand exoskeleton can restore intentional grasping in people with severe hand impairment by adding the missing motions needed for dexterous control. In practice, it enables meaningful daily tasks like feeding through a lightweight glove with wrist support and an active opposable thumb.
problem_solved: Severe hand paralysis can leave people unable to form functional grasps, even when some residual intent to move remains. This paper addresses the gap between motor intention and the limited physical articulation available for everyday hand use.
method: Design a lightweight textile-based hand exoskeleton that fits as a glove.
Add wrist dorsiflexion assistance to improve hand positioning for grasping.
Incorporate an active opposable thumb to increase hand articulations and enable more dexterous grasps.
impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this shows how intelligent assistive robotics can translate motion intent into real-world functional actions, improving quality of life beyond simple gesture recognition. It highlights the value of combining human-centered design, robotics, and control for high-impact rehabilitation systems.
visual_elements: Before/after illustration showing impaired hand vs. assisted grasping with the exoskeleton
Annotated glove diagram labeling wrist dorsiflexion support and active thumb mechanism
Step-by-step grasp sequence for a real task such as holding a spoon or feeding
Simple comparison graphic showing increased hand articulation with the device
paper_title: A dexterous soft hand exoskeleton restores intentional grasping in individuals with severe hand impairment
paper_authors: John Nassour, Nicolas Berberich, Daniel Utpadel-Fischler, Tobias Wächter, Gordon Cheng
